rv.q: It's funny but not quite irresistible - in the second half, the comic jeopardy of Bertie's scrapes starts to feel samey and on the wane.
Inventive design and a committed performance from Sam Harrison lift this meandering century-old comedy of manners
Sadly, the spectacle of Harrison’s rubber-man calisthenics don’t win extra sympathy for Bertie.
Harrison delivers each story beautifully, switching character to character at the snap of a finger and bringing each one of them onto the stage for the audience to meet and get to know.
For all its engaging and thoughtful elements, this is, however, a production that outstays its welcome.
For the rest, it feels like inconsequential nonsense that only PG Wodehouse fanatics would truly enjoy.
It is a master class in both performance and direction and set against an extremely attractive design buy Caite Hevner , with lighting by Tim Mitchell , of which more later.
Sam was brilliantly funny, absolutely charming and a delight to watch – I’m looking forward to enjoying his future work.
Anyone looking for a classic London night at the theatre cannot afford to miss this.
Jeeves Takes Charge is a charming, old-fashioned evening in the best sense of the phrase...
Jeeves Takes Charge is a bally good, one‑man delight.
It was truly an enjoyable evening, and the funniest performance I’ve seen for some time.
Jeeves Takes Charge is one of the most blissful marriages of richly humourous writing and uninhibited comic acting you are likely to see on the West End stage at any time.
Wodehouse’s brilliant turn of phrase and comedic flair is not in doubt, and this unadulterated dramatisation offers the full impact of his articulation and wit.
With clever staging and a mesmerising performance, Jeeves Takes Charge is full of laughs from beginning to end.
The most memorable trick of Jeeves Takes Charge is ultimately a theatrical one: one actor becomes an entire cast, and one room becomes an entire world.
A welcome return then for Wodehouse aficionados and perhaps a useful introduction for newcomers, this lavish production features a remarkable central performance.
Jeeves Takes Charge is a fun, very reverent take on the works of P.G Wodehouse, with a great physical performance from Sam Harrison.
Jeeves Takes Charge ultimately becomes an unusual contradiction: an astonishing central performance trapped inside a relatively unsuccessful revival.
I found the plot difficult to follow amidst the constant stream of text that becomes quickly exhausting, and hard to invest in.
Jeeves Takes Charge is a charming and cleverly staged piece of quintessentially British theatre.
A most charming, amusing and delightful escape from the outside world.
A highly enjoyable night at the theatre, and a chance to see some new (and old) reinventions of the classic characters many know so well.
Harrison draws us in with his vibrant performance and grasp of traditional comedy.
Jeeves Takes Charge might need some extra help to win the house over and eventually exploit its full potential.

Basic it was, but simple it wasn't. Caite Hevner ’s set design features a smart, minimalist drawing-room frame that relies heavily on projection-mapped backdrops to establish its various high-society settings. It perfectly transitions from place to place, heavily aided by the brilliant video design, also by Hevner .

Terrific physical comedy and Rupert Sadler’s incredible ability to shape-shift between characters is a lot of fun, but it does not deflect from an uneven script which will please old fans but struggle to keep the attention of new ones.
For newcomers, I’m less certain.
However, the lack of meaningful plot or character arcs means that, despite enjoying the play in the moment, it doesn’t leave much of a lasting impression.

cn.t: Sam Harrison's virtuosic one-man performance earns widespread praise in this Wodehouse adaptation, but critics are divided on whether the thin plotting and dated humor fully serve the material beyond nostalgic charm for existing fans.
